body.text: How Victoria's election campaign is playing out in regional electorates
Walk down the main street of any country town across Victoria and ask about politics and you will get very similar answers.
People feel that renewables projects have been approved without proper consultation, their hospitals are in chaos, and their roads are falling apart.
Many will mention that their community has missed out on funding while mega-projects race ahead in Melbourne.
And there is scepticism about the ability of the major parties to address the issues.
Regional Victorians have aired their grievances about a range of issues during this term of parliament.

On budget day in 2025, angry farmers and Country Fire Authority volunteers rallied on the steps of parliament about the Emergency Services and Volunteers Fund, which they said would increase their tax bills.

Tractors circled parliament house in August 2023 in protest about plans to build transmission lines across farmland in Victoria's west, which the Coalition has pledged to scrap and Labor has promised to review.

And potholes have become emblematic of regional frustrations, symbolised by the death of a motorcyclist who reportedly hit a pothole on the Western Highway, and a large pothole on the Princes Freeway in Gippsland that left 30 drivers with flat tyres.
On Saturday, November 28 voters will have their say on Labor's handling of these issues and whether they think the Coalition opposition can do better.
Complicating electoral calculations in regional Victoria is the rise of One Nation, which is riding a wave of voter disillusionment with the major parties.
See what the major issues are in your seat.
The state of play
Regional Victoria contributes 25 of the 88 seats which make up Victoria's lower house.
Those seats are split fairly evenly between Labor and the Coalition, with the government holding 11 to the Coalition's 14.
Labor draws much of its regional strength from the larger centres of Ballarat, Bendigo and Geelong, while the Coalition dominates in seats further away from Melbourne.

RedBridge Group pollster and director of strategy Kos Samaras told the ABC that Labor had held seats in those regional centres since Steve Bracks won the 1999 election, but this election he expected many of those seats would be lost to the Coalition.

"We expect a good chunk of them will [be lost], which will be a very different result to what the Labor Party was able to secure in 2010 when it did lose that election, where it was able to hold its provincial foothold and rebuild from that," Mr Samaras said.
"On this occasion, they will be losing seats in regional Victoria, that's for sure."
The ghosts of 1999
The last time there was widespread anger in regional Victoria was in 1999 when Jeff Kennett was seeking a third term.
Labor's Steve Bracks was little fancied going into the election with Mr Kennett expected to win in a canter.
But anger was simmering below the surface after seven years of privatisations and cuts to schools, hospital and transport.
The Coalition finished just short of a 45-seat majority, finishing with 43 seats to Labor's 42.
Regional Victoria was central to the outcome, with Labor picking up the seats of Ballarat East, Ballarat West, Bendigo East, Seymour and Narracan.
Mr Bracks formed minority government after securing the support of three rural independents, Craig Ingram in Gippsland East, Russell Savage in Mildura and Susan Davies in Gippsland West.
Major party decline
Fast forward 27 years and Labor is on the nose in regional Victoria and appears likely to lose government, if polling is accurate.
But anyone expecting a repeat of the 1999 result should not hold their breath.
Support for the major parties has declined since 1999, when Labor won 45.57 per cent of the primary vote to the Coalition's 47.02 per cent.
A RedBridge poll published in the Australian Financial Review on November 11 put support for the Coalition at 31 per cent with Labor at 23 per cent.
Surge in One Nation vote
A big part of what makes this election so different is the rise of One Nation.
It received 22 per cent of support in the RedBridge survey after securing a 2.04 per cent primary vote at the 2022 election.
But with the Coalition's vote improving as election day draws closer, Mr Samaras is not expecting an orange wave across regional Victoria.
One Nation's vote had dropped from the high 20s earlier this year to its current level, he said.
"That's a problem because One Nation needs a fairly high primary vote to remove a National Party MP or a Liberal Party MP who are occupying a regional electorate," Mr Samara said.
He said because of Australia's preferential voting system, One Nation would need a primary vote above 35 per cent in order to translate its support into seats.
"If they end up in most of these seats with a primary vote similar to that of the Coalition's, it'll be Labor preferences that actually elect the Coalition MP or candidate," Mr Samaras said.
He thinks that if One Nation wins anywhere, it will be in Morwell, which encompasses Victoria's coal heartland in the Latrobe Valley.
A Roy Morgan survey in October rated Morwell as the seat most likely to fall to One Nation.
"Basically, people [in Morwell] are of the view that whether it's the Coalition or whether it's the Labor Party, both have not really done the right thing by that part of Victoria," Mr Samaras said.

"It's an area that's obviously experienced significant industrial and economic decline and obviously the economic face of that part of Victoria has changed drastically and I think the politics will express that."
What's happening in your seat?
Bass
Labor had never held Bass until Jordan Crugnale seized it in 2018.
She managed to hold it in 2022 after an unfavourable redistribution, winning by a margin of 202 votes and making it the state's most marginal seat.
With Crugnale retiring, there is an expectation that the contest will be between the Liberals' Rochelle Halstead, a former mayor, and One Nation's Nikole Schellekens.
Former library chief executive Chris Buckingham is Labor's candidate this time around.

Located south-east of Melbourne, Bass is a mix of coastal communities at Inverloch and Phillip Island, farmers and a traditionally Labor-voting community in the regional centre of Wonthaggi. Roads, taxes on second properties and the economic effect of losing the Australian MotoGP to Adelaide are key issues.
The Liberals have been the key beneficiary from preference deals, with both Labor and One Nation placing Ms Halstead ahead of each other.
Bellarine
It was a changing of the guard in Bellarine at the 2022 election, with senior MP Lisa Neville's retirement making way for Alison Marchant to join parliament.
While Marchant ended up winning relatively comfortably, the 7.24 per cent swing against her in the primary vote will have some in the ALP sweating on this year's ballot.

The Liberals have not won an election here since Garry Spry went back-to-back-to-back in '99, but the team will be hopeful its candidate Callum Whitehead can benefit from a statewide drop in popularity for the incumbent government.
The question will be whether he can find enough voter support to erode an 8.5 per cent margin, or if Marchant has done enough in her first term for locals to give her another four years.

Despite having held the seat since 2002, there have been some close calls for the ALP in Bellarine along the way, so the much-discussed fall in popularity for Labor may make this yet another close contest.
Depending on who you talk to around the seat, this one could go either way, and should be one of the most interesting local seats for tally watchers come November 28.
Benambra
Liberal candidate Steve Martin has been busy on the campaign trail for 12 months in a bid to shore up the seat as Liberal MP, Bill Tiley, retires after 20 years.
But the 149-year conservative hold on the seat has loosened after strong independent campaigns in the last two Victorian elections whittled the Liberals' margin to under 1 per cent.
Now another independent is testing that slim margin as Wodonga-based GP Lachlan McKeeman challenges for the seat.
One Nation has put forward writer Kellie Sheppard to score some of the seat's conservative votes, while Labor and the Nationals are not fronting candidates.
The Liberals will be directing their Benambra preferences to One Nation, saying they favour those who back a change in government.

One Nation's Benambra how-to-vote card lists the Liberals fourth, but Kellie Sheppard told a recent election forum that she disagreed with the card, and personally wished for Libertarian candidate Tim Quilty and independent Dr McKeeman to have higher preferences as they more closely aligned with her values. Dr McKeeman is running an open ticket.

Health is a major issue in Benambra and the community has long criticised the controversial $558 million redevelopment of Albury's hospital, that operates under Victorian government jurisdiction and services the Benambra electorate.
Candidates generally agree the redevelopment will not meet the community's need and a new greenfield hospital is required, but have different plans on how and when that can be achieved.

The community has been angered during the election campaign after the Victorian opposition pledged more than $1 billion to Gippsland hospital projects, compared to $100 million to help relieve pressure at Albury.
Benambra residents also want better basic infrastructure, particularly roads.

The opposition has thrown money at Benambra in the months leading up to the election, which could win some votes, including $100 million for more beds at Albury Wodonga Health and $70 million to upgrades roads around Wodonga.
Bendigo East
Labor is attempting to retain the seat it has held through former premier Jacinta Allan for 27 years, with a new candidate in high school teacher Tim Rickwood.
Despite Labor holding the seat with a 10.91 per cent margin, Rickwood says he is the underdog.
Nationals candidate and publican Andrew Lethlean is already well known to voters, having challenged Labor for the federal seat of Bendigo at last year's election.
But unlike in other regional seats the National Party has not splashed major cash on election commitments, with local promises totalling about $10 million in Bendigo East.

Labor has focused its promises on health, education and transport, promising a free dental clinic, $18.5 million to the Bendigo Senior Secondary College, where Rickwood teaches, and an extra 101 extra services on the Bendigo V/line from 2028.
The National Party has never held Bendigo East, which has typically been a battle between Labor and the Liberals.
Bendigo West
Labor has held Bendigo West since 1996 and currently with a 14.35 per cent margin, but has an outgoing MP in Maree Edwards who is not recontesting after 16 years.
The Nationals are targeting Bendigo West with accountant and CFA volunteer David Hutchings, who has been campaigning alongside his more high-profile Bendigo East counterpart.
In this seat the Nationals' pledges have been small compared to other regions, about $3 million in total.

Labor's candidate Brenton Baldwin, who works in health policy, has announced $7.9 million for a primary school in the growing suburb of Maiden Gully, and joined his Bendigo East equivalent in announcing a free dental clinic for Bendigo, an extra 101 extra services on the Bendigo V/Line from 2028 and $18.5 million for the Bendigo Senior Secondary College.
Greens candidate Liza Shaw hails from Castlemaine, south of Bendigo, and is running an open ticket with no preferences except to put One Nation last.
The Greens have pledged to reinstate a V/Line stop at Harcourt, and Shaw is opposing a proposed McDonald's development in Castlemaine.
On the first day of early voting, Family First disendorsed its candidate Christos Harisopoulos after the ABC sent the party questions over content linked to him online.

Mr Harisopoulos said in a statement that several people in the party were "fully aware" of his parody accounts online, and while he holds no animosity towards Family First, he'll be voting for One Nation.
Eildon
Eildon is another electorate that was badly hit by the 2026 bushfires, affecting towns such as Alexandra and Fawcett in the Murrindindi Shire.
The shire was one of the hardest-hit local government areas, with substantial damage to farm fencing, infrastructure and homes.
Murrindindi Shire has been advocating for more bushfire recovery funding from the state and federal governments, saying that it has received only 10 per cent of all funding allocated to councils.
The electorate has been held by the Liberals, with the incumbent, Cindy McLeish, seeking re-election.
Community independent Tom Ward has also entered the race and his campaign was launched by former Indi MP Cathy McGowan and Queensland MP Bob Katter.
Ward was one of many who lost his family home in the January bushfires and has committed to giving half his annual salary to community groups if elected.
Eildon is also home to the town of Mansfield, which has been vocal on health policy in recent years, especially on the issue of merging local hospital boards in 2024.
The town is en route to Mount Buller and has been advocating for a new ambulance station, which has been given a $3.8 million commitment from the Liberals.
Eureka
Created via redistribution in 2022, Eureka stretches from Melbourne's western fringe to Ballarat's eastern edge in what has traditionally been a Labor heartland.
It is held by Agriculture Minister Michaela Settle, who convincingly won what is considered one of the most racially diverse seats in regional Victoria.
Nine candidates are vying for the seat and tensions have been high.
Earlier this month, a hotel, corflutes and cars were targeted with anti-One Nation graffiti. The party's candidate Paul Ballinger condemned the move.
He also urged his supporters to put Victorian Socialists candidate Andy Raven last, while the incumbent Ms Settle wants voters to put Mr Ballinger last.
Meanwhile, Liberal candidate Emma Muir is hoping to flip the seat, with a campaign focused on getting a "fair deal" for regional Victoria.
Euroa
The electorate was badly affected by the 2026 bushfire season. The Longwood blaze destroyed more than 150 structures and led to the loss of one life.
It destroyed most of the buildings in the small town of Ruffy as well as hundreds of agricultural properties in the electorate.

In the aftermath of the blaze, only two buildings, the Ruffy fire shed and town hall, remained on the town's main street. Recovery has been front of mind for residents in the regions, with local councils heavily advocating for disaster funding and tax relief.

The Strathbogie Shire has called on all sides of politics to commit to three years of rates relief and a three-year deferral of the controversial emergency services and volunteers levy for fire victims.

Euroa also includes the township of Benalla, home to major manufacturing such as the munitions factory run by Thales and timber manufacturer ForestOne, which closed its dry sawmill and particleboard manufacturing operations in the town.
The electorate has been held by the Nationals since 2014 and the current member Annabelle Cleeland is seeking re-election.
She and One Nation's Steve Campbell have listed Family First's Moussa Taouk second on their how-to-vote cards.
Geelong
Labor has not lost an election in Geelong since winning by the barest of margins, 16 votes, in 1999, and the feeling around town is that incumbent MP Christine Couzens should hold on once again.

A poor campaign by the Liberal Party in 2022 saw Ms Couzens win her third term by the largest margin (14.71 per cent) the electorate has seen since the 50s, increasing her stranglehold by 4.4 per cent on the previous election, where she faced down celebrity independent Darryn Lyons.
The Liberals appear to have learned their lessons from the last two elections, unveiling prominent local bar owner Andy Pobjoy, known as Geelong's "Piano Man", as their candidate back in July.

Suggestions of a statewide swing against Labor would not be in the least bit surprising in Geelong, where the government has failed to deliver on numerous previous election pledges, from the Commonwealth Games and fast rail to finding a new home for key CBD homelessness charity The Outpost.
John De Lorenzo is a relatively strong candidate for One Nation, as is Emilie Flynn for the Greens, both of whom had a crack at the federal seat of Corio last year.
But the question for many in Victoria's second city is whether a 14.71 per cent margin will be too great to overcome for any serious challengers to Ms Couzens.
Gippsland East
Covering a large regional area that includes towns such as Bairnsdale, Lakes Entrance, Paynesville, Orbost and Omeo, Gippsland East has traditionally been a conservative stronghold.
The area's economy is closely linked to agriculture, fishing, tourism associated with the Gippsland Lakes, farming and forestry.
The current Labor government's policy to bring forward the closure of the native timber industry hit small communities in the region hard, with towns such as Swifts Creek and Orbost affected.
The National Party has historically held the seat.
This long-standing streak was interrupted in 1999 when independent MP Craig Ingram won the seat and retained it until 2010, when the Nationals' Tim Bull reclaimed it.
Bull held the seat at the 2014, 2018 and 2022 elections, before announcing his retirement.
Local primary school teacher Gemma Rendell has been nominated as his successor.
Steve Goodman is the One Nation candidate, with recent polling showing a surge in support for the party.
Roads and regional infrastructure are key issues, with the East Gippsland Shire Council seeking a $1.5 billion statewide roads package.
Health care, particularly upgrades to the Bairnsdale Hospital and better access to doctors, is also a priority.
In Lindenow, a proposed minerals mine is a divisive issue, particularly among those seeking to attract new industry and the local horticultural sector.
Gippsland South
Gippsland South is traditionally one of Victoria's safest National Party seats.
It is a large electorate that covers areas such as Sale, Leongatha, Korumburra, Mirboo North, Wilsons Promontory, and Port Albert.
The Nationals and its precursor, the Country Party, have held the seat continuously since 1982.
Sitting MP Danny O'Brien is the party's leader, and has held the seat since a 2015 by-election, when he replaced former deputy premier Peter Ryan.
The region's economy is heavily dependent on agriculture, particularly dairy, forestry, fishing, mining and tourism.

Major issues for the region including operating costs and workforce shortages for farmers, water security and impacts of changing energy policies, health care and access to doctors, roads and infrastructure, and regional industries associated with forestry.
Labor's decision to stop native timber harvesting also affected towns such as Yarram.
Lara
Labor has had a stranglehold on Lara since the seat was created in in 2002 to replace the abolished seat of Geelong North, also held by Labor since its 1967 creation.
Ella George took over from previous longstanding MP John Eren in 2022, and won comfortably.
Despite a loss of 8.2 per cent in the primary vote, George still took 49.7 per cent of all votes.

The numbers do not look great for any serious challenge from the Liberal Party, which may be why candidate Tim Beddoe seemed to have been the least active of the Liberal challengers in the Geelong region during the early stages of the campaign period.

One sticking point for many locals in the region has long been a feeling that the seat is so safe that it is often overlooked when it comes to government spending by Labor, but the party seems to be responding this election cycle with a late flurry of big-money pledges.
Taking in much of Geelong's northern suburbs, Lara has traditionally been seen as the blue-collar heart of the region.
The disappearance of Labor's blue-collar base has been spoken about for the past decade or more, meaning a potential swing towards conservative parties could be on the cards.
But, dethroning an MP who took almost half of the first preference votes four years ago seems a little too steep of a hill to climb.
Lowan
Lowan is a seat largely isolated from the cut and thrust of overt political campaigning.
Even as early voting begins, corflutes are scarcely populated around the electorate's population hub, Horsham.
They have relative abundance in surrounding towns such as Halls Gap, Hamilton and Casterton, but are far less plentiful than in neighbouring electorates.
Lowan is the state's largest seat geographically, and close contests are particularly rare.
It has been held by Nationals deputy leader Emma Kealy since 2014.
Ms Kealy polled 58.85 per cent of first preferences at the 2022 election, close to triple her nearest opponent.
Labor is often a distant second in the vote.
But the Nationals had a vice-like grip on first preference votes in 2022, winning all 53 polling booths in Lowan.
Eight candidates are contesting the seat in 2026, including a comedian, a former mayor, educators, a civil engineer, and a wool industry veteran.
One Nation is expected to garner support through its candidate Andrew Partridge, a former local who now resides in Geelong.
A reborn Australian Democrats party has put forward Karen Hyslop, who until recently was the mayor of Northern Grampians Shire.

Labor and Family First have nominated teachers Sue Pavlovich and Lee-Ann Elmes, and the Greens candidate is former road construction engineer Jeff Moran, who contested the federal seat of Corio in 2016 as a Bullet Train for Australia candidate.

Mineral sands, transmission lines and renewable energy projects are prominent election issues, as is housing availability, childcare access, mental health access, neighbourhood house funding security and the emergency services levy.
Macedon
Labor has held Macedon since its inception in 2002 but current MP Mary-Anne Thomas is not recontesting.
There are three former Macedon Ranges Shire mayors in the running: Annette Death for Labor, Kate Kendall for the Liberals and Dom Bonanno, the 2022 Liberal candidate, as an independent.
Mr Bonanno stood down as mayor after being caught drink driving and speeding in a council car last year.
The Labor government's fast-track planning policy has been controversial in the electorate for pushing through housing developments, despite the opposition of the council and some community members.

Ms Kendall has pledged to return a planning decision on a new township at Clarkefield to local council, and to remove a controversial planning overlay in Lancefield, while Ms Death and Mr Bonanno have both pledged to advocate on planning issues.
Both Labor and the Coalition have committed to upgrading the Tony Clarke Reserve in Macedon and the Urquhart and High St intersection in Woodend.
The Liberals have also pledged a $12 million upgrade to the Daylesford Hospital and several school projects.
Labor has committed to several upgrades, including $16 million for Riddells Creek Primary School, $7.8 million for Daylesford Aged Care, and $2.2 million for stage 1 of the Hanging Rock masterplan.
Mr Bonanno has preferenced One Nation ahead of the major parties and has committed to advocate for upgrades to Daylesford hospital and Lancefield Park.
Mildura
Mildura will likely come down to a contest between two candidates.
Sitting Nationals MP Jade Benham has the task of fending off the rising popularity of One Nation, represented in the seat by fresh-faced agribusinessman Guy Cooper.
Ms Benham, Mr Cooper and Greens candidate Katie Clements were the only three candidates who attended the electorate's lone election forum in Mildura.
Mildura is an expansive state seat, where issues transform the further you travel from Sunraysia.
For those in the main population centre, hospital improvements and passenger rail remain perennial talking points, while crime has become a hot button issue.
Outside of Mildura, energy policy and road maintenance are issues of focus.

The absence of former Mildura MP Ali Cupper from the ballot has shifted the tone of the election from a once-tantalising prospect of a three-corner contest to a contest of ideas between conservative candidates.
How Ms Cupper's expected vote is dispersed may decide the winner.
The Greens, Animal Justice Party, Socialists and Labor all preference the Nationals above One Nation on their how-to-vote cards.
Family First preferences One Nation above the Nationals.
One Nation has pledged to scrap net zero targets, secure land for a new Mildura Base Public Hospital, and is supportive of the return of passenger rail.
The party also proposed lowering the criminal age of responsibility to 10 and making families of youth offenders pay for damages to property.
Ms Benham is eyeing off a cabinet position in a Coalition government.
Mildura has never had a cabinet minister in its history.
The Nationals have made election promises to restore passenger rail to Mildura, upgrade Mildura Base Public Hospital, and make burglary and robbery serious offences under the Bail Act.
Morwell
A Labor stronghold for 36 years until the Nationals snatched it in 2006, Morwell is now among the seats firmly in One Nation's sights.
The electorate covers Victoria's coal-power heartland of the Latrobe Valley and includes the towns of Moe, Morwell and Traralgon.
The region has grappled with high unemployment since the local power stations were privatised in the 1990s.
That was followed by the closure of the Hazelwood power station in 2017 with the Yallourn power station set to follow in 2028.
This election, jobs and employment remain the biggest issue, particularly in light of the looming closure of Yallourn.
Crime is also a key issue, with residents and businesses expressing concerns about safety in the Morwell CBD.
Russell Northe held the seat for the Nationals from 2006 to 2017, when he resigned from the party to sit on the crossbench.
Mr Northe retired ahead of the 2022 election, when Martin Cameron won it back for the Nationals and now holds it on a 4.4 per cent margin.
This election, he is facing Tracie Lund, a former independent and Morwell Neighbourhood House manager, who is now representing Labor, and One Nation's Casey Murphy.
In October, polling company Roy Morgan ranked Morwell as the most "winnable" seat for One Nation.
Labor has preferenced the Coalition ahead of One Nation, which could make the difference in a tight contest.
Murray Plains
Murray Plains is held by the Nationals with a very safe 22.89 per cent margin, but is considered up for grabs for One Nation.
A recent visit to the electorate by leader Pauline Hanson was a sign of the party's optimism.

There's a sense of disillusionment with the major parties in this rural electorate over decaying roads, the fallout of water reform, and the imposition of renewable projects onto agricultural communities.
The electorate borders communities over the Murray River in NSW that voted in One Nation MP David Farley in the Farrer by-election this year.
Murray Plains Nationals MP Peter Walsh is retiring after 24 years and former Victorian Farmers Federation president and Quambatook farmer Brett Hosking is hoping to take his place.
His main contender is former Gannawarra Shire mayor Garner Smith for One Nation, who has been outspoken in his council role on VNI West, renewables and water policy.
The Nationals have pledged up to $100 million to replace the single-lane Swan Hill bridge, a project the community has long been advocating for.
One Nation and the Nationals have preferenced each other third, both putting Family First second on their how-to-vote cards, followed by Labor in fourth.
Narracan
For most of its existence, Narracan has been the Liberal Party's heartland in Gippsland.

Taking in the growing regional hubs of Warragul and Drouin, plus farming and smaller communities in the Baw Baw Baw Shire, it has been held by the Liberals for almost its entire history since its creation in 1967.
The only break came in 1999, when Ian Maxfield won it for Labor at the election which brought Steve Bracks to power.
It reverted to the Coalition in 2006, when Liberal Gary Blackwood won the seat.
Mr Blackwood retired ahead of the 2022 election, but the death of the Nationals candidate ahead of polling day meant that the election in Narracan was abandoned.
Builder Wayne Farnham won the seat at a supplementary election in January 2023 with 51.69 per cent after preferences, after Labor decided not to field a candidate.
This time, he is up against Labor's Jannette Langley and popular Baw Baw Shire councillor Ben Lucas, who is representing One Nation.
The major issue in Narracan is ensuring Warragul and Drouin have the infrastructure they need as they grow.
At the top of the community's wishlist is a new hospital to replace the aging West Gippsland Hospital.
The Coalition has promised a new hospital at every election since 2018, with Labor matching the promise ahead of the 2022 poll.
But aside from some funding for planning in the 2023 budget, development on the project has stalled.
The Coalition has recommitted to the project this election, promising a 230-bed hospital as part of its promise to spend a quarter of new infrastructure spending on projects in regional Victoria.
Ovens Valley
This picturesque seat is very safe Nationals country, taking in towns such as Bright, Cobram and Wangaratta.

But this deeply conservative pocket, held by Nationals MP Tim McCurdy, could also be ripe for fed-up residents to hand their votes to One Nation, which has fronted 32-year-old food relief worker James Rouel.
Labor, which scored 20 per cent of the first preference votes in 2022, is running Jen Smith, who works in retail and hospitality.
Mr McCurdy's preferences will flow to One Nation, which has instead prioritised Libertarian and Family First candidates ahead of the Nationals. Labor has put One Nation last.
Energy is a hot topic in the electorate, with residents airing their frustration over the establishment of large-scale renewable projects.
Communities have been left angered by what they say is a lack of consultation and their inability to appeal renewable developments, which some candidates argue swallow up prime agricultural land.
The Emergency Services and Volunteers Fund has also sparked fury locally since it was announced by the state government.
The Coalition and One Nation have pledged to scrap the tax, with the opposition saying it will restore the former Fire Services Property Levy model if elected.

The opposition's pledges to help retain the seat include $10 million to redevelop Yarrawonga College, $5 million to upgrade Cobram Football Netball Club, $4 million to fight fruit fly, and $4 million to establish a dedicated dialysis facility at Cobram.
Polwarth
One of Victoria's largest seats by land area, Polwarth covers a varied swathe of Victoria's south-west, with Colac at its heart, Torquay to its east and stopping just short of Terang to the west.
The Liberals' Richard Riordan is the incumbent MP, having first won the seat at a by-election in 2015, carrying on the tradition of Polwarth effectively being a Liberal seat since 1950.

But the booming populations of Torquay and other seachange towns along the Surf Coast have brought a left-leaning swing to recent elections, with Greens and Labor voters narrowing Riordan's margin to a 52 per cent to 48 per cent two-party preferred win over Labor's Hutch Hussein in 2022.
Labor probably feels it might be able to get over the line eventually as the populations in Torquay, Anglesea and Lorne grow, particularly if preferences push them along.
The combined Labor/Green vote in 2022 was 46 per cent of first preferences versus Riordan's 42.5 per cent.
But Labor needs a really strong candidate and a bit of luck to overcome the strong rural Liberal vote, with Ms Hussein returning in the hope that the second time's a charm for Labor.
On the other side of the political pendulum, the purported rise of One Nation and reduction of Labor could see Riordan extend his margin.
There are plenty of promises in Polwarth, but the most consequential may be the one that hasn't been kept.

In 2018, Labor promised it would build a community hospital in Torquay to provide greater access to urgent care for the booming coastal community, but eight years later the project seems all but abandoned, with little explanation from the government.
In the section of Polwarth where Labor most needs to maintain its support, an empty paddock where a new hospital was meant to be built may be too bitter of a pill to swallow for many voters.
Ripon
Starting between Ballarat and the Grampians and extending north through prime Western District farmland, Ripon has long been a hotly contested seat.
The electorate has bounced between Labor and Liberal for its entire existence, with incumbent Labor MP Martha Haylett wresting it from two-term Liberal MP Louise Staley in 2022 by a tight margin.
Ripon will again be a busy race, with 12 candidates in the running, including the only Coalition duel in the state, with the Liberal and Nationals both fielding hopefuls.
But with its older population, comparative lack of diversity, and low education and income rates, experts see it as ripe for the picking for ascendant One Nation candidate Donna Buxton.
Buxton was announced as a candidate at a "Farmers Fightback" rally in Marnoo headlined by Pauline Hanson, in her only Western District appearance so far in the campaign.
As with many regional and rural Victorian seats, the VNI West and the Western Renewables Link high-voltage transmission line projects are a key issue.
One Nation, the Liberals and the Nationals have promised to either pause or cancel both projects, with Labor pushing ahead.
The emergency services fund, public transport and affordable housing are also key issues, while Liberal candidate Megan Read has also been critical of the state of the electorate's roads.
Last week, Labor MP Martha Haylett accused Central Goldfields Shire of "dramatically" mismanaging the now-closed Maryborough outdoor pool, suggesting the mayor and CEO "reconsider their positions".

The Maryborough pool has become a mini-battleground within the wider war for the hearts and minds of Ripon, with the Liberals, Nationals and Labor promising $5 million, though Labor's promise comes with "very strict conditions" on Central Goldfields Shire.
Shepparton
The Shepparton electorate encompasses Victoria's food bowl, stretching from the heart of the Goulburn Valley all the way to the Victoria-New South Wales border.
It has been a Nationals and Country Party stronghold since its creation except for two terms between 2014 and 2022 where it was held by independent Suzanna Sheed.
The Nationals won back the seat in 2022 with the election of former Shepparton mayor Kim O'Keeffe.

It encompasses the towns of Shepparton, Strathmerton and Numurkah. Food manufacturing forms a key part of its economy with operations in the region including SPC, Campbell's soup, GrainCorp and until recently Bega, which closed its Strathmerton site in 2025, leading to the loss of 300 jobs.
The region also experienced significant property damage during the devastating floods in 2022 and the affordability of disaster insurance remains a key issue for locals.
The Nationals have preselected high-profile Shepparton Mayor Shane Sali as their candidate to face off the wave of support for One Nation, who have pre-selected the relatively unknown Phil Bryant.

The electorate's history as a marginal seat means there is significant support for Shepparton to return to an independent, with the Voices for Goulburn Valley movement nominating Lou Costa as its candidate.
Both One Nation and the Nationals have preferenced Family First second.
South Barwon
South Barwon is looking worse and worse for the Labor Party as the election gets closer.

It won back-to-back elections here with Darren Cheeseman, but it has been an embarrassing term for both the government and MP, who was effectively booted from the party in early 2024 over "persistent inappropriate behaviour" and sent to the crossbench.
Since then he has stayed on as an MP, collecting a handy salary and benefits despite ongoing criticism over a severe lack of contribution to the role.

A South Barwon loss in confidence in the Labor Party would not be surprising, meaning fresh ALP candidate Rebecca Thistleton will have her work cut out to woo voters from looking back to the Liberal Party, or One Nation.

Labor's struggling popularity locally has been further exacerbated by the government's failure to deliver on previous election promises, including a new high school for Mount Duneed and new ambulance and fire stations in Armstrong Creek.

In 2018, the Labor Party promised to build a new fire station for the growth area following a fatal house fire, and is yet to break ground on the project. Another fatal Armstrong Creek house fire this month has put a deeply tragic emphasis on the lack of action on this unfulfilled promise.
Despite these issues, and an expected statewide swing against Labor, there is a good bit of ground to make up for any real challenge from the Liberal candidate Libby Pettit.
While tipsters have Ms Pettit in the box seat, Labor's saving grace may be preference flows from the Greens if they take a good slice of votes leaking from disillusioned Labor voters on November 28.
South-West Coast

South-West Coast stretches from the Great Ocean Road hamlet of Peterborough to the South Australian border, taking in the regional city of Warrnambool and some of the state’s richest dairying country.
A Liberal stronghold, South-West Coast is held by shadow cabinet secretary Roma Britnell, who claimed 58 per cent of the two-party preferred vote in 2022.

The electorate's demographic is older, with lower income, education and cultural diversity than the rest of the state on average, traits that some experts say make it vulnerable to a One Nation swing.
In the 2022 election, it was a 10-way race, with four independents running taking over 25 per cent of the vote.
This time around there are no independents, raising questions about where that massive chunk of votes will go.

Mr Hughes, a former detective, is seen as one to watch, though it's hard to see Ms Britnell's popularity being shaken enough to take the seat out of Liberal hands for the first time since it was created in 2002.
Wendouree
Amid the statewide storm of government disenfranchisement, regional Victoria's smallest seat must seem like a lighthouse of stability for Labor.
Made up of Ballarat suburbs, the seat has been held by Labor MP Juliana Addison since 2018 and is seen as one of the few Labor sure bets this election.
Ms Addison won with 61.9 per cent of the two-party preferred vote in 2022, and with the Liberals starting from so far behind, they will need a big swing.
Public transport has been a hot topic in Wendouree, with Labor promising 550 new services across the Geelong, Ballarat and Bendigo corridors, and to cap costs at $30 a week.
Opposition leader Jess Wilson declined to match this promise, citing the current state of Victoria's finances.
Crime, particularly car theft, is another hot button issue for the electorate, and one Liberal candidate Gavin Ronan is promising to address.
The Liberals and Nationals have promised to recruit an additional 3,000 police officers across the state, compared to Labor's pledge of 1,500 new recruits.
Wendouree also houses Ballarat Base Hospital which, like many regional hospitals, has struggled with emergency department pressures and burnout.
One Nation has been critical of Labor's $655 million budget to improve the hospital, saying it will likely cost up to $1 billion and calling it another of Labor's "usual lies and broken commitments".
